newsitem.title: UK: Rpt-UK's FTSE braces for huge options trade expiry.
newsitem.headline: Rpt-UK's FTSE braces for huge options trade expiry.

text.p: The deadline for London's biggest-ever single options trade, in a cocktail of futures and options expiry on Friday, looks set to lead the UK stock market down a very turbulent path.
"It's going to be one of the biggest expirations we've ever had," said one derivatives trader. "People are getting very nervous of the market and volatility has already skewed up."

As the deadline drew near, speculation mounted over how the anonymous investor, who set up the billion-pound plus derivatives strategy in November, intends to unwind, what is now assumed to be a deal that has gone horribly wrong.
The decision could play a significant role in where the market heads, in the short term at least.

"There's one billion pounds ($1.6 billion) worth of stock tied up against those options that needs to be unwound," said one dealer. "It could have a substantial impact on the market and we may see some aggressive trading."
Market insiders suggested the investor was most likely to be one of Britain's large life assurance companies trying to protect the value of its stock portfolio in the event of a market crash.
But as well as buying downside protection, the investor chose to cut the cost of the deal by selling 35,000 June 4,300 calls at the same time.
The call position carried the risk of unlimited losses if the FTSE 100 were to rise above 4,300. At the time the deal was struck, the leading UK stock index stood at 3,900.
The calls alone accrued losses of 350,000 stg for every point the FTSE rose above the 4,300 level.
"You would have thought that he'd have closed the position by now, given the levels we've seen the market rise to," one options specialist commented.
Nervousness is compounded by the market's recent swings as rumours of a cut in the corporate tax credit on dividend payments have taken their toll.
Volatility, as measured by the FTSE 100's 10-day moving average, has spiked higher as the blue chip index fell around 150 points from its all-time peak of 4,783, reached just four days ago.
Derivatives traders have suggested that recent falls in stock prices could be related to the options position.
"Some of us suspect he is already unloading stock, by the way the market has been performing this week," one dealer said.
Dealers said this week people on the opposite side of the deal have already begun to take up their rights to cash in on the contracts.
But 24,000 of the June 4300 calls, with an underlying value of 1 billion stg, still remain open.
"There is a lot of talk that he may have hedged against these potential losses, say on the OTC (over-the-counter) market, which could have neutralised his position," one dealer said.
"But we really have no idea who took out the trade and why they did it."
The unusually large number of positions in the June FTSE 100 futures, where open interest was nearly 40,000 contracts, may also be related to the options deal.
The risk will come if the calls expire and the portfolio is not covered. The investor may then have to off-load stock before settlement.

"Everyone is talking about this trade," said a senior options dealer, "but unless it's exercised early we just won't know what is going to happen until the game unwinds on Friday between 10.00 and 10.30(0900GMT/0930GMT)."
June FTSE index futures and options contracts expire at 0930 GMT on Friday.
